entries.content:
It is difficult to put into words the full extent of what I felt during the experiment. The pain itself was sharp, immediate, and inescapable—each shock seemed to strip away another layer of my composure, leaving me raw and exposed. But what lingered even more than the physical sensation was a profound sense of betrayal. I found myself searching the faces of those administering the shocks, hoping for some sign of hesitation, some flicker of empathy, but there was only the cold machinery of procedure and authority. It reminded me, painfully, of that moment described by Dr. Lanyon, when horror and disbelief mingled with a kind of sickened curiosity—except this time, I was the subject, not the observer.

Emotionally, I felt a growing distrust—not just toward those in positions of power, but toward the very idea that people will do what is right when instructed otherwise. The authority figures, whom I might have trusted to intervene or show mercy, instead became distant, almost spectral presences, their commands more real than my suffering. It left me with a sense of disillusionment, much like the soul-sickened terror Lanyon described after witnessing something that shattered his faith in the order of things. I find myself questioning whether the bonds of trust and decency are as strong as I once believed, or if, as Jekyll discovered, the temptation to obey or to harm is always lurking, ready to surface when the circumstances allow.

I am left unsettled, wary, and changed. The experiment has made me more cautious, less willing to accept authority at face value, and more aware of the darkness that can emerge in ordinary people under pressure.
